IMAGE PROMPTING · 10 MIN

How to Write AI Image Prompts Like an Art Director.

A practical system for subject, composition, light, lens and production constraints.

Published September 3, 2026Editorial team · PromptStudio AI

Useful image prompts are creative briefs, not adjective collections. The goal is to make a small number of compatible visual decisions that a model can execute and a human can evaluate.

IN THIS GUIDE1. Begin with the job of the image2. Build the prompt in production order3. Use camera language only when it changes the result4. Protect what must not change

Begin with the job of the image

Before describing style, state what the image must accomplish. A marketplace packshot needs accurate geometry and clear edges. A campaign hero needs emotion, hierarchy and space for copy. A headshot needs trust and identity fidelity. The same visual treatment cannot serve all three jobs equally well.

Write one sentence that names the subject, audience and destination. For example: “A landing-page hero for a premium coffee subscription aimed at design-conscious urban professionals.” That sentence becomes the test for every later choice.

Build the prompt in production order

A reliable order is subject, setting, composition, lighting, material or styling, camera, output format and constraints. This mirrors how a photographer or art director would make decisions. It also lets you revise one layer without rewriting everything.

Keep the subject concrete. Replace “a beautiful product photo” with the product type, material, color and immutable details. Replace “cinematic lighting” with direction, softness, contrast and color temperature. Specific decisions produce more testable results than prestige words.

Use camera language only when it changes the result

Lens and aperture descriptions can guide framing and depth, but they are not magic quality commands. A 24mm lens suggests a wider spatial relationship; an 85mm lens suggests portrait compression; a macro lens suggests close detail. Choose the language because it supports the job.

Aspect ratio is equally important. Decide whether the image is for a square marketplace listing, a 4:5 social post, a 16:9 thumbnail or a wide website hero before generating. Reframing later can destroy the composition.

Protect what must not change

Editing prompts should separate protected source details from editable decisions. For a product, protect shape, label, color and included parts. For a person, protect identity, age, skin tone and natural features. For architecture, protect the real floor plan and view.

Review output at full resolution. Check hands, eyes, text, logos, edges, reflections and repeated patterns. A visually impressive thumbnail can still contain errors that make it unusable commercially.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Define the commercial job first.
  • Use a repeatable production order.
  • Choose camera and ratio intentionally.
  • State immutable details explicitly.
  • Review at full resolution.
